title: Spot the AI
about: Tell apps that follow written rules from AI that learns from examples.

cards.title: AI is already in your pocket
cards.body:
Your phone unlocks when it sees your face. Most programs follow **rules** a person wrote: at 7:00, ring the alarm. Nobody could write rules for every face, so face unlock learns from lots of **examples** instead.

In this course, **artificial intelligence (AI)** means software that learns from examples, called **machine learning**.

cards.prompt: Does each one **follow rules** someone wrote, or **learn from examples**?
cards.hint: Ask: could a person write down every step exactly? If yes, it follows rules.
cards.nudge: Look again at the jobs that must cope with things nobody planned, like a new face.
cards.explanation: Alarms, calculators and timed lights follow exact rules. Face unlock, spam filters and keyboard suggestions **learn from examples**: there are too many faces, emails and sentences for rules.

cards.prompt: Which job is easiest to solve by **learning from examples**?

options.nudge: Adding follows a few exact rules. Which job has endless variety?
That's one simple rule. Which job has millions of different cases?

options.text: Turning the lights off at midnight
options.nudge: One timer rule can do that. Which job has examples that all look different?

cards.hint: Which job has endless variety, where no two examples look the same?
cards.explanation: Everyone's handwriting is different, so nobody could write rules for it all; a computer learns from examples instead. Adding, alarms and timers need just a few exact rules.

cards.prompt: Match each kind of [[AI|artificial-intelligence]] to the examples it learns from.
cards.hint: Ask: what would it need to see lots of to get good at its job?
cards.nudge: Ask what each one is trying to guess, and which examples would show it.
cards.explanation: Each one learns from examples of its own job: songs you **skip and replay**, **scans of your face**, emails **marked as spam**, and words people **usually type next**.

cards.prompt: Trickier: does each one **follow rules**, or **learn from examples**?

items.label: A heater that adapts to your routine
A game enemy on a set path
An enemy that copies top players' moves
A photo app that finds dogs

cards.hint: Ask: did someone write every step in advance, or does it improve by noticing what happens?
cards.nudge: Some pairs look alike: did a person write the steps, or did it learn from examples?
cards.explanation: A timer, a set path and a converter follow exact rules. The adapting heater, the copying enemy and the dog finder **learn from examples**. The same job can be done either way.

cards.prompt: When [[AI|artificial-intelligence]] recognises your face, does it **understand** you like a friend does?

options.text: Yes: it knows you just like a friend does
options.nudge: A friend knows your jokes and favourite food. What did the AI learn from?

options.text: Partly: it knows your name, but not your feelings
options.nudge: Face unlock never needs your name. What did it actually learn from?

options.text: No: it matches patterns learned from examples
No: it looks up your name online each time
options.nudge: It doesn't look anything up. How did it learn to recognise you?

cards.hint: Think back to how AI learns: from examples.
cards.explanation: Face unlock matches **patterns** in your face to examples it learned. It doesn't know who you are or how you feel, which is why AI can be fooled.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Ordinary programs follow **rules** a person wrote.
- **AI** learns from **examples** instead, finding patterns. That's **machine learning**.
- It matches patterns. It doesn't understand things like people do.

Next: you'll teach a model yourself.
